text: In the mid-eighteen hundreds, the most powerful leader among them was a man named Cochise, of the [Chokonen](/ʧoʊkˈoʊnən/) band, whose people lived around Apache Pass and the mountains to the west.
Somewhere in Missouri, as one of those trains labored up a steep grade, a man named [Massai](/mæsˈaɪ/) jumped.

[Massai](/mæsˈaɪ/) had been an Army scout. He was on the train anyway. According to the story his family later told, he became convinced the prisoners were going to be killed, and he chose to run. Traveling at night, he made his way back across hundreds of miles of unfamiliar country to the mountains of the Southwest.

Around nineteen oh six, [Massai](/mæsˈaɪ/) was killed by a posse in New Mexico. His daughter, Alberta Begay, later shared the family's memories with historian Eve Ball. Her mother's words, near the end of her life, were simple: "Your father was not a murderer. He killed only to protect us."

Today the highest viewpoint you can drive to in the park is called [Massai](/mæsˈaɪ/) Point. Even the Park Service admits the name may rest on a mistaken settler story about a horse thief. The family that ran the nearby ranch asked that it be named for him anyway.
But in the years [Massai](/mæsˈaɪ/) was hiding in the mountains, those same valleys were filling with a different kind of fugitive.

A decade later, in the depths of the Great Depression, a camp of young men from the Civilian Conservation Corps arrived. They built roads, trails, a tunnel, a fire lookout and the stone overlook at [Massai](/mæsˈaɪ/) Point. At one point, seventeen of them worked barefoot because their shoes hadn't arrived, until a telegram to a U S senator finally got them boots.
